name: Komo, also Kumu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Thomas, John Paul. 1992. Tone in Komo. Work Papers of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, University of North Dakota Session 36: 71-160. DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol36.04 (UND Scholarly Commons; duplicate ERIC scan ED351879).
catalog_locator: §2.1 'Nouns', p. 76 (volume pagination; running header 'page 76 / Thomas' with footer 'SIL-UND Workpapers 1992'); §3.4 'Digression: tone-bearing units', pp. 93-94; identity §1.1 p. 72.
catalog_quote: In most Komo nouns, each syllable has a discrete, level tone. The following table lists the possible tones on two syllable nouns, each line representing a possible combination of tones, as indicated in the leftmost column. In the representations that follow, an acute accent indicates a high tone; the lack of an accent indicates a low tone. ... Thus, all possible combinations, or melodies, of the two tones, high and low, are attested in bisyllabic nouns. In monosyllabic nouns, however, an additional tone appears: a rising contour. ... The problem then concerns accounting for the rising tone. Here, I analyze it as being a combination of an L tone and an H tone. [p. 76] ... In the discussion so far, I have assumed that only vowels are tone-bearing units. In fact, not only vowels, but also nasals can bear tone in Komo. This is most evident in the rare cases where nasals bear high tones. [p. 93]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.citation: Thomas, John Paul. 1992. Tone in Komo. Work Papers of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, University of North Dakota Session 36: 71-160 (DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol36.04; ERIC ED351879).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the UND Scholarly Commons PDF, DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol36.04; 91 form-feed pages). The running header 'SIL-UND Workpapers 1992 / page 76 / Thomas' precedes section '2 Komo lexical tone / 2.1 Nouns', and the passage reads verbatim: 'In most Komo nouns, each syllable has a discrete, level tone. The following table lists the possible tones on two syllable nouns.. In the representations that follow, an acute accent indicates a high tone; the lack of an accent indicates a low tone.. Thus, all possible combinations, or melodies, of the two tones, high and low, are attested in bisyllabic nouns. In monosyllabic nouns, however, an additional tone appears: a rising contour.' (…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Komo is a two-tone language (H vs L, with a rising contour on monosyllables) in which every syllable, and some nasals, carries a discrete lexical or grammatical tone; the tone monograph, the 1992/2011 segmental morphophonology and the 2014 dictionary phonology page never mention word stress, accent or prominence, so no stress rule is stated anywhere in the accessible descriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress. Tonal notes: rare high-toned nasals; word-initial nasals before voiceless obstruents get default L (whistle test, pp. 93-94).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described at word level (nouns, verb stems) and at derivational, inflectional and post-lexical (phonological-phrase) strata; nothing on stress at any domain. The 'accent' occurrences are the acute diacritic for H tone, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Komo/Kumu of DRC, Bantu D.23 (Guthrie), ISO kmw, glottocode komo1260, data from the Maniema/Haut-Zaire (Tshopo, Lubutu-Punia-Walikale) area; no dialect named. Not to be confused with Koman Komo of Ethiopia/Sudan (komo1258, ISO xom): Glottolog's Yehualashet 2014 'Orthography of Komo' (Lissan) belongs to komo1258 and is misfiled under this language.

new_statements.quote: Le komo se sert de trois signes de ton, l'accent aigu, l'accent macron et l'accent circonflexe. L'accent circonflexe s'emploie rarement. [...] L'accent aigu indique un ton haut. Dans d'autres langues, l'accent grave indique un ton bas. Donc, si le ton monte dans une syllabe, c'est comme joindre un accent grave avec un accent aigu. [...] S'il n'y a pas d'accent sur une syllabe, celle-ci peut porter n'importe quel ton selon l'exigence du mot et de la phrase où la syllabe en question se trouve.
new_statements.translation: Komo uses three tone signs, the acute accent, the macron accent and the circumflex accent. The circumflex accent is rarely used. [...] The acute accent indicates a high tone. In other languages, the grave accent indicates a low tone. So if the tone rises within a syllable, it is like joining a grave accent with an acute accent. [...] If there is no accent on a syllable, that syllable can carry any tone according to the requirement of the word and of the sentence in which the syllable in question occurs.
new_statements.citation: Thomas, J. Paul. 1986. Rapport sur le système d'orthographe komo; Projet de langue komo. SIL archive entry 32369.
new_statements.locator: §4 'Les signes de ton', pp. 6-7 (document and PDF pagination coincide; 18-page PDF)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (18 pp., born-digital, Author metadata 'John Paul Thomas', title 'Rapport sur le système d'orthographe komo'). extracted text shows document page numbers 6/7/8 at the top of PDF pages 6/7/8, so the paginations coincide. §4 'LES SIGNES DE TON' begins on p. 6 with 'Le komo se sert de trois signes de ton, l'accent aigu, l'accent macron et l'accent circonflexe. L'accent circonflexe s'emploie rarement.' then 'L'accent aigu indique un ton haut. Dans d'autres langues, l'accent grave indique un ton bas. Donc, si le ton monte dans une syllabe, c'est comme joindre un accent grave avec un accent aigu.' and, at the top of p. 7, 'S'il n'y a pas d'accent sur une syllabe, celle-ci peut porter n'imp…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement from Thomas 1992 'Tone in Komo' (tone language with level H/L tones per syllable, no stress statement); the 1994 orthography statement (same author, J. Paul Thomas, with Katinga Mbokani and Omari Musalia; SIL dates it 1986-1994, PDF version 2010) confirms a two-tone system with contour tones from H+L sequences and adds nothing on stress. The SIL record dates the work 1994 (created 1986-1994), not 1986 as in the listed citation. archived copy (Internet Archive, 31 Jul 2024) after sil.org returned a not reachable by automated download for the PDF.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The orthography statement treats Komo as a tone language: every syllable bears a tone (high, low, rising or falling), 'accent' marks in the text mean tone diacritics (acute = high, macron/hacek = rising, circumflex = falling), and tone is written only where it is grammatically or lexically distinctive (verb prefixes/tense, 3pl object, the associative á, minimal pairs such as bhomá 'fendre' vs bhómá 'insulter'). Nothing is said about word stress or prominence; the only prosodic remark beyond tone is that question intonation changes from the start of the sentence (§6.2, p. 15).
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; tone marking is optional where context disambiguates (§4 (7), p. 8)
new_statements.identity_note: Both works concern Komo/Kumu of DR Congo (ISO kmw, Bantu D.23), the Komo language project of SIL Eastern Zaire Group (Thomas's orthography was developed with Katinga Mbokani and Omari Musalia); not the Koman Komo of Ethiopia (komo1258). The compendium introduction lists Komo in a proposed 'Komo Group' (Komo, Bhele, Kaiku, Bila, Bira, Kwamba/Humu) within Bira-Huku D.30 on lexicostatistic grounds.

sources.note: Dedicated 90-page tone study: Komo has two level tones H and L (plus a rising contour on monosyllables), every syllable carries a discrete level tone, nasals can be tone-bearing, three strata of tone rules, downstep, intonation. The words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur except 'acute accent' as a tone-marking diacritic (pp. 76, 82); nothing is said about word stress or prominence.

tone.says: Unpublished SIL (Nairobi) overview of four related languages, Bera (D32), Bila, Bele (D31) and Komo (D23); Thomas 1992 'Tone in Komo' cites it only for that grouping (p. 72) and not for any tone fact, so its tone coverage of Komo is unknown. Kutsch Lojenga separately checked Thomas's tone paradigms (p. 75).

tone.quote: (4) Kimasa word game examples (High tones are marked with acute accent; low tones are unmarked) … Also note that the tones stay with the same position in the word that they started with. This shows the relative independence of tones and segments. You can move whole syllables around and the tones stay in the same relative position, as autosegmental phonology would predict. … In the Kimasa game, the nasals move just as any other syllable, and take tone just as any other syllable. So this data shows these nasals are syllabic nasals.
tone.locator: pp. 4-5, section 3 'Komo—Democratic Republic of Congo', data sets (4)-(6)
tone.summary: Marks high (acute) vs low (unmarked) tone on Komo syllable-reversal game forms after Thomas 1992; tones keep their position when syllables move, syllabic nasals bear tone; no analysis of the system.
tone.says: Marks high (acute) vs low (unmarked) tone on Komo syllable-reversal game forms after Thomas 1992; tones keep their position when syllables move, syllabic nasals bear tone; no analysis of the system.
